questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman with a penicillin allergy has community-acquired pneumonia with lobar consolidation. Sputum Gram stain shows lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci. Her physician wants an oral fluoroquinolone that reliably covers this organism and atypical pathogens, and that can also be used if she later develops a urinary tract infection.

Which fluoroquinolone fits best?
choices: Levofloxacin, a respiratory agent with good streptococcal coverage
Ciprofloxacin, because it has the strongest Gram-negative activity of the class
Moxifloxacin, because it has the greatest anaerobic activity of the class
Ciprofloxacin, because poor urinary levels are not a concern in pneumonia
Moxifloxacin, because it is renally excreted and reaches high urine levels

explain.html:
The fluoroquinolones split by streptococcal coverage and by how they leave the body. Ciprofloxacin has poor streptococcal coverage, so it is not indicated for community-acquired pneumonia. Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin are the respiratory fluoroquinolones, active against S. pneumoniae and atypicals. The class is renally excreted except moxifloxacin, which is hepatically metabolized and does not reach adequate urinary concentration, so it cannot treat a UTI.

Lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci are S. pneumoniae, which rules out ciprofloxacin. The extra requirement that the same drug could treat a later urinary infection rules out moxifloxacin. Only levofloxacin satisfies both, which is why it is one of the preferred drugs for community-acquired pneumonia in a penicillin-allergic patient.
why: Ciprofloxacin's Gram-negative strength does not help here because it has poor streptococcal coverage and is not used for pneumonia.
Moxifloxacin covers pneumococcus but is hepatically metabolized and cannot treat the urinary infection the physician also wants covered.
The problem with ciprofloxacin in pneumonia is weak S. pneumoniae activity, not urinary levels, which are adequate.
Moxifloxacin is the one fluoroquinolone that is not renally excreted, so the stated reason is false.
explain.takeaway: Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin are respiratory fluoroquinolones that cover S. pneumoniae; ciprofloxacin does not reliably cover it, and moxifloxacin cannot treat a UTI because it is not renally excreted.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Recommend appropriate antibiotic therapy based on site of infection and suspected or actual bacterial pathogens

rows.if_right: a complicated UTI or Pseudomonas infection

rows.if_right: an intra-abdominal infection or pneumonia where anaerobic coverage matters and no UTI is expected

rows.if_right: a urinary tract infection caused by an Enterobacterales species

rows.why: Moxifloxacin is the one fluoroquinolone that is not renally excreted, so the stated reason is false.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old man has Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis. Given alone in the laboratory, gentamicin barely affects the isolate, and ampicillin alone only slows its growth. When the two are combined, the culture is killed rapidly. The same gentamicin dose readily kills Pseudomonas aeruginosa without any partner drug.

Which explanation best accounts for the rapid killing with the combination?
choices: Gentamicin inhibits the beta-lactamase that degrades ampicillin in enterococci
Ampicillin damage to the cell wall increases gentamicin entry to the 30S ribosomal subunit
Ampicillin and gentamicin bind two different sites on the 50S subunit together
Gentamicin blocks efflux pumps that would otherwise remove ampicillin
The combination blocks two sequential steps in bacterial folate synthesis

explain.html:
Aminoglycosides irreversibly bind the 30S subunit, interfere with the initiation complex and cause misreading of mRNA, which produces nonfunctional or toxic proteins and is bactericidal. Getting to the ribosome is the limiting step: used alone, aminoglycosides have only Gram-negative activity, including Pseudomonas. Against Gram-positives such as Enterococcus and S. aureus, they are given with a cell wall agent for synergy, because beta-lactams or vancomycin increase aminoglycoside entry into the bacterium.

The vignette shows exactly that split: gentamicin alone kills Pseudomonas but barely touches E. faecalis, while ampicillin plus gentamicin kills the enterococcus rapidly. Ampicillin damages the wall, and gentamicin then reaches its 30S target. This is the basis of the classic ampicillin plus gentamicin regimen for enterococcal endocarditis.
why: Aminoglycosides do not inhibit beta-lactamases; the synergy comes from improved drug entry, not enzyme protection.
Gentamicin binds the 30S subunit, and ampicillin does not bind ribosomes at all.
Aminoglycosides are not efflux pump inhibitors, and ampicillin's site of action is the cell wall, not the cytoplasm.
Sequential folate blockade describes sulfamethoxazole plus trimethoprim, not a cell wall agent plus an aminoglycoside.
explain.takeaway: Aminoglycosides alone cover only Gram-negatives; against Gram-positives such as Enterococcus they work synergistically with cell wall inhibitors, which increase aminoglycoside entry to the 30S ribosome.
explain.topic: Aminoglycoside synergy with cell wall agents
explain.subject: Pharmacology

rows.if_right: a beta-lactamase inhibitor such as clavulanate restoring ampicillin activity

rows.why: Gentamicin binds the 30S subunit, and ampicillin does not bind ribosomes at all.
rows.if_right: two protein synthesis inhibitors that both act at the 50S subunit

rows.why: Aminoglycosides are not efflux pump inhibitors, and ampicillin's site of action is the cell wall, not the cytoplasm.
rows.if_right: an experimental efflux pump inhibitor that lowers the MIC of several drugs at once

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant has a cough and is diagnosed with atypical pneumonia. A clinician considers a drug that reversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA from attaching to the A site. A colleague advises against it in this patient.

Which adverse effect is the main reason to avoid this drug class in pregnancy?
choices: Irreversible ototoxicity of the developing inner ear
Neural tube defects from folate antagonism
Neonatal jaundice from displacement of bilirubin
Interstitial nephritis of the fetal kidney
Staining and deformity of developing teeth

explain.html:
Tetracyclines reversibly bind the 30S subunit and block aminoacyl-tRNA attachment at the A site, which halts elongation and is bacteriostatic. They cover atypical organisms, which is why one was considered for her pneumonia. Their listed adverse effects are hepatotoxicity, chelation of cations, photosensitivity, esophagitis and staining or deformity of teeth (tetracycline mostly). Because developing teeth take up the drug, the lecture states plainly to avoid tetracyclines in pregnancy.

The mechanism in the stem names the class, and the 14-week pregnancy makes the fetal tooth effect the deciding concern. An alternative with atypical coverage should be chosen instead. The other choices are real toxicities of other drugs.
why: Ototoxicity belongs to aminoglycosides, which bind 30S irreversibly, not to tetracyclines.
Folate antagonism is the trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole mechanism, not a tetracycline effect.
Tetracyclines do not cause neonatal jaundice; their pregnancy warning is staining and deformity of developing teeth.
Interstitial nephritis is not a tetracycline effect; it is the signature of nafcillin.
explain.takeaway: Tetracyclines reversibly bind 30S to block aminoacyl-tRNA at the A site, and they stain and deform developing teeth, so they are avoided in pregnancy.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Recognize major or very common side effects

rows.why: Ototoxicity belongs to aminoglycosides, which bind 30S irreversibly, not to tetracyclines.
rows.if_right: a drug that binds the 30S subunit irreversibly and causes misreading of mRNA

rows.why: Folate antagonism is the trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole mechanism, not a tetracycline effect.
rows.if_right: a drug that inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase

rows.why: Tetracyclines do not cause neonatal jaundice; their pregnancy warning is staining and deformity of developing teeth.
rows.if_right: a newborn given ceftriaxone, which causes hyperbilirubinemia and neonatal jaundice

rows.why: Interstitial nephritis is not a tetracycline effect; it is the signature of nafcillin.
rows.if_right: a patient on nafcillin who develops rash, fever and a rising creatinine

questions.stem:
A 61-year-old man in a long-term care facility has a wound infection with several resistant organisms. The lab reports MRSA, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE), an ESBL-producing Klebsiella, and a fourth isolate. The team chooses a glycylcycline because it covers resistant Gram-positives, ESBL producers and anaerobes, but a pharmacist warns that one isolate will not be covered.

Which fourth isolate would this drug miss?
choices: Acinetobacter baumannii
Bacteroides fragilis
Proteus mirabilis
Streptococcus pyogenes
Escherichia coli

explain.html:
The glycylcyclines, tigecycline and eravacycline, extend the tetracycline spectrum to resistant organisms. They cover Gram-negatives including ESBL producers and Acinetobacter, Gram-positives including MRSA and VRE, anaerobes and some mycobacteria. Their gaps are summarized as the "4 Ps": no Pseudomonas, no Proteus, no Providencia and no Morganella (formerly Proteus). That is why they are used for resistant infections such as MRSA, VRE and ESBL Gram-negatives.

In this wound the team already knows the drug covers MRSA, VRE and the ESBL Klebsiella. Of the choices, only Proteus mirabilis sits in the 4 Ps, so it is the isolate left uncovered. In practice, a mixed infection that includes one of the 4 Ps needs a second agent.
why: Tigecycline covers Acinetobacter, including resistant strains, so this isolate would be treated.
Tigecycline has anaerobic activity, so Bacteroides would be covered.
Tigecycline covers Gram-positive cocci, including resistant ones like MRSA and VRE.
Tigecycline covers Gram-negatives such as E. coli, including ESBL producers.
explain.takeaway: Tigecycline and eravacycline cover MRSA, VRE, ESBL producers, Acinetobacter and anaerobes but miss the 4 Ps: Pseudomonas, Proteus, Providencia and Morganella.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Describe the general spectrum of activity

rows.why: Tigecycline covers Acinetobacter, including resistant strains, so this isolate would be treated.
rows.if_right: an isolate of Pseudomonas or Providencia

rows.why: Tigecycline has anaerobic activity, so Bacteroides would be covered.
rows.if_right: a regimen with no anaerobic activity, such as an aminoglycoside alone, facing Bacteroides

rows.why: Tigecycline covers Gram-positive cocci, including resistant ones like MRSA and VRE.
rows.if_right: a patient on aztreonam alone, which has no Gram-positive activity, facing S. pyogenes

rows.why: Tigecycline covers Gram-negatives such as E. coli, including ESBL producers.
rows.if_right: an isolate of Morganella, one of the 4 Ps

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old man with a deep neck abscess from an infected molar is treated with an oral drug that binds the 50S subunit, inhibits peptidyl transferase and is chosen because it covers Gram-positive cocci including MRSA as well as oral anaerobes. Ten days later he has 8 watery stools daily, crampy abdominal pain and a white blood cell count of 18,000/microL (normal 4,500 to 11,000). Colonoscopy shows yellow-white plaques on the colonic mucosa.

Which statement about the antibiotic he received is correct?
choices: It is intrinsically active against most Gram-negative rods
It is the oral drug of choice for this patient's colitis
It acts at the 30S subunit and is bactericidal against all MRSA
It shows no cross-resistance with macrolide antibiotics
It covers anaerobes and toxin makers but not Gram-negatives

explain.html:
Clindamycin, a lincosamide, binds the 50S subunit and inhibits peptidyl transferase, blocking elongation; it is bacteriostatic. Its spectrum is Gram-positives including MRSA, anaerobes, and an anti-toxin effect against toxin-producing Gram-positive organisms. It has no Gram-negative activity because Gram-negatives are intrinsically resistant, and resistance is common, including cross-resistance with macrolides. It is used for skin and soft tissue, oropharyngeal and ENT infections.

A deep neck abscess from a molar is exactly where Gram-positive and oral anaerobic coverage matters, which is why clindamycin was chosen. Ten days later he has watery diarrhea, leukocytosis and yellow-white plaques, which is C. difficile pseudomembranous colitis, the adverse effect most strongly tied to clindamycin. The drug caused the colitis; it does not treat it.
why: Gram-negatives are intrinsically resistant to clindamycin, so the statement is false.
Clindamycin is the cause of pseudomembranous colitis, not its treatment.
Clindamycin binds the 50S subunit and is bacteriostatic, so both parts of the statement are wrong.
Cross-resistance between clindamycin and macrolides is specifically noted, so the statement is false.
explain.takeaway: Clindamycin inhibits peptidyl transferase at the 50S subunit, covers Gram-positives including MRSA, anaerobes and toxin producers, has no Gram-negative activity, and is a leading cause of C. difficile colitis.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Describe the general spectrum of activity

rows.if_right: a Gram-negative rod infection treated with a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin

questions.stem:
A 55-year-old man with peptic ulcer disease from Helicobacter pylori is started on triple therapy that includes a macrolide. He also takes a drug for which small increases in blood level cause toxicity. Two days later his level of that drug has nearly doubled. His physician notes that switching to azithromycin would likely have avoided this interaction, though azithromycin is not the agent used in triple therapy.

Which macrolide was most likely prescribed, and what explains the interaction?
choices: Azithromycin, by chelating the drug in the gut
Clarithromycin, by inhibiting hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
Erythromycin, by speeding gastric emptying
Clarithromycin, by blocking renal tubular secretion
Fidaxomicin, by binding bacterial RNA polymerase

explain.html:
Macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin) bind the 50S subunit and block translocation of the growing peptide from the A site to the P site; they are bacteriostatic. They cover streptococci, atypicals, Chlamydia, Legionella, Bordetella and MAC prophylaxis, and clarithromycin is the macrolide in H. pylori triple therapy. The interaction to know is CYP inhibition, especially with erythromycin and clarithromycin, which raises levels of other drugs metabolized by those enzymes. Azithromycin has much less of this effect. Erythromycin is also used for GI motility, a separate property.

Triple therapy for H. pylori means clarithromycin, and a narrow-window drug whose level nearly doubles within two days points to hepatic enzyme inhibition. That is why the physician notes azithromycin would have spared the interaction. Check for interacting drugs before starting clarithromycin.
why: Azithromycin is not the triple therapy macrolide, and gut chelation is a tetracycline problem, not a macrolide one.
Erythromycin speeds GI motility, but it is not the triple therapy agent and faster emptying would not double a drug level.
Clarithromycin's interaction runs through hepatic CYP enzymes, not renal tubular secretion.
Fidaxomicin binds RNA polymerase and is used only for C. difficile, not in triple therapy.
explain.takeaway: Clarithromycin is the macrolide in H. pylori triple therapy, and erythromycin and clarithromycin inhibit CYP enzymes and raise levels of other drugs, while azithromycin does so much less.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Recognize clinically important antibiotic drug-drug interactions

rows.why: Azithromycin is not the triple therapy macrolide, and gut chelation is a tetracycline problem, not a macrolide one.
rows.if_right: a patient taking doxycycline with antacids

rows.why: Erythromycin speeds GI motility, but it is not the triple therapy agent and faster emptying would not double a drug level.
rows.if_right: a patient with gastroparesis given erythromycin for motility

rows.why: Clarithromycin's interaction runs through hepatic CYP enzymes, not renal tubular secretion.
rows.if_right: a drug interaction described as reduced renal excretion of a second drug

rows.why: Fidaxomicin binds RNA polymerase and is used only for C. difficile, not in triple therapy.
rows.if_right: a patient with recurrent C. difficile colitis

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old woman has her third episode of Clostridioides difficile colitis in 4 months. Each prior episode responded to treatment but returned. Her physician chooses a macrocyclic agent that is used exclusively for this infection and is more effective at preventing recurrence. Unlike other drugs in its broad structural family, it does not act on the ribosome.

Which step does this drug block?
choices: Translocation of the growing peptide chain on the 50S subunit
Reduction of a nitro group to toxic free radicals in anaerobes
Formation of the 70S initiation complex at the 23S rRNA
Supercoiling of DNA by DNA gyrase during replication
Opening and closing of the RNA polymerase clamp at transcription initiation

explain.html:
Fidaxomicin is a macrocyclic macrolide that, unlike classic macrolides, does not act on the ribosome. Its target is bacterial RNA polymerase: it binds the switch region and prevents the enzyme from properly opening and closing the DNA clamp. That blocks transcription initiation and halts mRNA synthesis. It is used exclusively for C. difficile infection and is more effective at preventing recurrences; its main adverse effect is GI disturbance.

A third C. difficile episode in 4 months and a drug chosen to prevent recurrence identify fidaxomicin. The stem's note that it spares the ribosome separates it from azithromycin and its relatives, which block translocation on the 50S subunit. Recurrence prevention is the clinical reason to reach for it.
why: Blocking translocation on the 50S subunit is how classic macrolides act, and the stem says this drug does not act on the ribosome.
Nitro group reduction to free radicals is the metronidazole mechanism, and metronidazole is a nitroimidazole, not a macrocyclic agent.
Blocking the 70S initiation complex at the 23S rRNA is linezolid, a ribosomal agent.
DNA gyrase is the fluoroquinolone target, and fluoroquinolones can cause C. difficile rather than prevent its recurrence.
explain.takeaway: Fidaxomicin binds the switch region of bacterial RNA polymerase to block transcription initiation, is used only for C. difficile, and better prevents recurrence.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

rows.why: Blocking translocation on the 50S subunit is how classic macrolides act, and the stem says this drug does not act on the ribosome.
rows.if_right: a macrolide such as azithromycin used for atypical pneumonia

rows.why: Nitro group reduction to free radicals is the metronidazole mechanism, and metronidazole is a nitroimidazole, not a macrocyclic agent.
rows.if_right: a nitroimidazole prodrug activated inside anaerobes

rows.why: Blocking the 70S initiation complex at the 23S rRNA is linezolid, a ribosomal agent.
rows.if_right: an oxazolidinone used for VRE or MRSA

rows.why: DNA gyrase is the fluoroquinolone target, and fluoroquinolones can cause C. difficile rather than prevent its recurrence.
rows.if_right: a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin

questions.stem:
In a laboratory study of Escherichia coli, drug X alone blocks formation of dihydrofolic acid and only slows growth. Drug Y alone blocks the conversion of dihydrofolic acid to tetrahydrofolic acid and also only slows growth. Given together, the two drugs kill the bacteria. Human cells are much less affected because they take up preformed folate rather than synthesizing it.

Which pair of enzymes do drugs X and Y inhibit, in order?
choices: DNA gyrase, then topoisomerase IV
Dihydrofolate reductase, then dihydropteroate synthase
Dihydropteroate synthase, then dihydrofolate reductase
Peptidyl transferase, then RNA polymerase
Thymidylate synthase, then dihydropteroate synthase

explain.html:
Bacteria must build their own folate, so the folate pathway is a selective target. Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, which blocks formation of dihydrofolic acid. Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, the later step that converts dihydrofolic acid to tetrahydrofolic acid. Blocking two sequential steps starves the cell of the folate it needs for DNA synthesis, and the synergy makes the combination bactericidal even though each drug alone is weaker.

In the experiment, drug X acts first (making dihydrofolic acid) and drug Y acts at the conversion to tetrahydrofolic acid, and only the pair kills. That order is sulfamethoxazole then trimethoprim. This is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, used for skin infections and PCP.
explain.table:
StepEnzymeDrug
Formation of dihydrofolic acidDihydropteroate synthaseSulfamethoxazole
Dihydrofolic to tetrahydrofolic acidDihydrofolate reductaseTrimethoprim
ResultSequential blockadeBactericidal together
why: DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV are fluoroquinolone targets in DNA replication, not folate synthesis.
This pair reverses the order: dihydropteroate synthase acts first and is the sulfonamide target.
Peptidyl transferase and RNA polymerase are the clindamycin and fidaxomicin targets, unrelated to folate.
Neither drug targets thymidylate synthase, and dihydropteroate synthase acts before dihydrofolate reductase.
explain.takeaway: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; the sequential blockade of folate synthesis makes the combination bactericidal.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

rows.why: DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV are fluoroquinolone targets in DNA replication, not folate synthesis.
rows.if_right: two drugs that block DNA supercoiling and chromosome separation

rows.why: This pair reverses the order: dihydropteroate synthase acts first and is the sulfonamide target.
rows.if_right: drug X blocking the conversion to tetrahydrofolic acid and drug Y blocking dihydrofolic acid formation

rows.why: Peptidyl transferase and RNA polymerase are the clindamycin and fidaxomicin targets, unrelated to folate.
rows.if_right: one drug blocking peptide bond formation and another blocking transcription initiation

questions.stem:
A 74-year-old man on long-term oral prednisone for polymyalgia rheumatica is treated for a complicated urinary tract infection with an oral drug that has excellent bioavailability (oral nearly equal to intravenous) and strong Gram-negative and Pseudomonas activity but poor streptococcal coverage. On day 5, while stepping off a curb, he feels a sudden pop at the back of his right ankle and cannot rise onto his toes.

The drug that caused this injury kills bacteria by inhibiting which target?
choices: The 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of messenger RNA
DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication
Dihydrofolate reductase, blocking the last step of folate synthesis
Penicillin-binding proteins, blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking
Bacterial RNA polymerase, blocking the start of transcription

explain.html:
Fluoroquinolones kill bacteria by inhibiting DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II), the main target in Gram-negatives, and topoisomerase IV, the main target in Gram-positives. Blocking these enzymes stops DNA replication and repair, so killing is concentration dependent and bactericidal. The class has excellent bioavailability (oral nearly equal to intravenous) and is renally dose adjusted. Ciprofloxacin is the member with strong Gram-negative and Pseudomonas activity but poor streptococcal coverage, which is why it is used for urinary infections and not for community-acquired pneumonia.

The decisive finding here is the sudden pop at the heel on day 5 in an older man on prednisone: Achilles tendon rupture, the fluoroquinolone musculoskeletal toxicity flagged especially in the elderly and in patients on steroids. Recognizing the drug from its profile and its toxicity leads straight to its target. Clinically, this is a reason to avoid fluoroquinolones for simple infections when a safer drug works.
explain.table:
AgentCoverageKey use or limit
CiprofloxacinStrong Gram-negative and Pseudomonas, poor streptococcalUTI, prostatitis, traveler's diarrhea; not for CAP
LevofloxacinGood S. pneumoniae, some PseudomonasPreferred fluoroquinolone for CAP
MoxifloxacinGood Gram-positive and anaerobes, no PseudomonasRespiratory and intra-abdominal; not for UTI
why: Misreading of mRNA at the 30S subunit is the aminoglycoside mechanism, and aminoglycosides are not oral agents that cause tendon rupture.
Dihydrofolate reductase is the trimethoprim target, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is not linked to tendon rupture.
Penicillin-binding proteins are the beta-lactam target, and the tendon toxicity points to a fluoroquinolone instead.
RNA polymerase is the fidaxomicin target, and fidaxomicin is used only for C. difficile, not urinary infections.
explain.takeaway: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV and cause tendinopathy and tendon rupture, especially in elderly patients taking corticosteroids.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 63-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who takes an antiarrhythmic drug is started on levofloxacin for pneumonia. On day 2 an outpatient physician, unaware of the first prescription, adds a second antibiotic that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks translocation, to cover Mycoplasma. That evening she faints, and telemetry shows a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with twisting QRS complexes.

Which shared effect of the two antibiotics best explains this event?
choices: Hyperkalemia from blockade of sodium channels in the distal nephron
Direct histamine release that causes vasodilation and hypotension
Serotonin excess from weak inhibition of monoamine oxidase
Delayed cardiac repolarization that prolongs the QT interval
Neuromuscular blockade that weakens the respiratory muscles

explain.html:
Several antibiotics inhibit cardiac repolarization and lengthen the QTc interval, and the effect is additive. Fluoroquinolones carry this cardiac toxicity, with torsades de pointes as its dangerous end point, and the lecture warns about it especially with macrolides and calls for caution and closer monitoring with antiarrhythmics. Macrolides prolong the QT on their own as well, so stacking the two classes on an antiarrhythmic compounds the risk.

The second drug binds the 50S subunit, blocks translocation and was added for Mycoplasma, so it is a macrolide such as azithromycin. Syncope with polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and twisting QRS complexes is torsades. Clinically, check the medication list for other QT-prolonging drugs before adding a macrolide to a fluoroquinolone.
why: Hyperkalemia is listed for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, not for fluoroquinolones or macrolides, and it does not produce twisting QRS complexes.
Infusion-related histamine release is the vancomycin infusion syndrome, and neither drug here causes it.
Weak monoamine oxidase inhibition belongs to linezolid, and serotonin excess causes clonus and fever, not torsades.
Neuromuscular blockade is an aminoglycoside toxicity and would cause weakness or respiratory depression, not a ventricular arrhythmia.
explain.takeaway: Fluoroquinolones and macrolides both prolong the QT interval, and combining them, especially with an antiarrhythmic, risks torsades de pointes.
explain.topic: QT prolongation with fluoroquinolones and macrolides
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Recognize clinically important antibiotic drug-drug interactions

rows.if_right: a patient on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole with a rising potassium

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis and chronic kidney disease is treated for Pseudomonas bacteremia with a bactericidal drug that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit irreversibly and has a narrow therapeutic window requiring drug-level monitoring. Over the course of therapy the team worries about several toxicities.

Which set of adverse effects should the team monitor most closely with this drug?
choices: Tendon rupture, QT prolongation and photosensitivity
Tooth staining, esophagitis and hepatotoxicity
Thrombocytopenia, optic neuritis and lactic acidosis
Ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity and neuromuscular blockade
Creatine kinase elevation, myopathy and eosinophilic pneumonia

explain.html:
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) are bactericidal 30S inhibitors with a small therapeutic window, so drug levels are monitored to prevent toxicity. Their class-wide adverse effects are three: ototoxicity, auditory and vestibular and possibly irreversible; nephrotoxicity as acute tubular necrosis; and neuromuscular blockade, which can cause flaccid paralysis or respiratory depression. Nephrotoxicity is worse with other nephrotoxins, chronic kidney disease and older age. Neuromuscular blockade is worse with neuromuscular blockers and in myasthenia gravis.

Irreversible 30S binding plus level monitoring identifies the drug, and this patient has both risk amplifiers: chronic kidney disease and myasthenia gravis. The team should follow levels, renal function, hearing and respiratory strength. Each distractor is a real toxicity set, just from a different class.

ClassSignature adverse effects
AminoglycosidesOtotoxicity, nephrotoxicity (ATN), neuromuscular blockade
FluoroquinolonesTendon rupture, QT prolongation, photosensitivity, CNS effects
TetracyclinesHepatotoxicity, photosensitivity, esophagitis, tooth staining
LinezolidThrombocytopenia, serotonin syndrome, neuropathy, lactic acidosis
DaptomycinCK elevation (monitor CK)
why: Tendon rupture, QT prolongation and photosensitivity are fluoroquinolone effects, not those of a 30S binder.
Tooth staining, esophagitis and hepatotoxicity are tetracycline effects; tetracyclines bind 30S reversibly and are bacteriostatic.
Thrombocytopenia, optic neuritis and lactic acidosis are linezolid effects, and linezolid acts at the 50S subunit.
CK elevation is the daptomycin monitoring concern, and daptomycin depolarizes membranes rather than binding the ribosome.
explain.takeaway: Aminoglycosides cause ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis) and neuromuscular blockade, with higher risk in chronic kidney disease and myasthenia gravis.

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man returns from camping in North Carolina with fever, headache and a petechial rash that began on the wrists and ankles and spread to the trunk, including the palms. He recalls removing a tick. He is started on the drug of choice for this infection. He usually takes it with his morning glass of milk and an over-the-counter antacid for heartburn.

What is the main concern with how he is taking the drug?
choices: Divalent cations in milk and antacids chelate it in the gut
Milk and antacids speed its renal clearance and require a higher dose
Antacids raise gastric pH and convert the drug to a toxic metabolite
Calcium in milk precipitates the drug in the bile and causes sludging
Milk proteins bind the drug in plasma and prevent it from entering cells

explain.html:
Tetracyclines are intracellular killers: they penetrate cells, which makes them effective against rickettsiae, chlamydia and mycoplasma. Doxycycline is the drug of choice for most infections caused by rickettsiae and Borrelia, including Rocky Mountain spotted fever and Lyme disease. Their absorption has a well-known weak point: tetracyclines chelate divalent cations, so milk, antacids and iron supplements bind the drug in the gut and less of it is absorbed. They are hepatically eliminated and do not reach urine or CSF well.

A tick bite followed by fever, headache and a petechial rash spreading from wrists and ankles to the trunk and palms is Rocky Mountain spotted fever, so he is on doxycycline. Taking it with milk and an antacid every morning undercuts absorption. He should separate doses from dairy, antacids and iron.
why: Tetracyclines are mostly hepatically eliminated, and the interaction happens in the gut before absorption, not in the kidney.
Raising gastric pH does not create a toxic doxycycline metabolite; the cations themselves bind the drug.
Biliary precipitation with calcium is not a tetracycline problem; the calcium interaction here is chelation in the gut.
The interaction is chelation in the gut lumen, not binding to milk proteins in plasma.
explain.takeaway: Doxycycline is the drug of choice for rickettsial infections such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and tetracyclines chelate divalent cations in milk, antacids and iron, which blocks absorption.
explain.topic: Doxycycline for rickettsial disease and chelation

explain.objective: Recognize clinically important antibiotic drug-drug interactions

questions.stem:
A 47-year-old woman with depression treated with sertraline is admitted with a complicated skin infection caused by vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium. She is started on a bacteriostatic drug that binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and prevents formation of the 70S initiation complex. Two days later she is agitated and diaphoretic, with a temperature of 38.8 C (101.8 F), heart rate 124/min, tremor, hyperreflexia and inducible clonus.

Which property of the antibiotic best explains her new findings?
choices: It has weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor activity
It inhibits hepatic cytochrome enzymes and raises sertraline levels
It prolongs cardiac repolarization and causes sympathetic surge
It suppresses the marrow and causes fever from neutropenia
It causes lactic acidosis that stimulates the nervous system

explain.html:
Linezolid, an oxazolidinone, binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and prevents formation of the 70S initiation complex. It is bacteriostatic against most Gram-positives and covers MRSA, VRE and penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae. Its most important interaction is serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic agents, because linezolid has weak MAOI activity. Its other adverse effects are thrombocytopenia after about 2 weeks, peripheral neuropathy and optic neuritis, and rarely lactic acidosis.

She takes sertraline, starts linezolid for VRE, and within two days has agitation, fever, tachycardia, tremor, hyperreflexia and inducible clonus, the picture of serotonin syndrome. Clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin excess rather than to any other linezolid toxicity. Before starting linezolid, check for SSRIs and other serotonergic drugs.
explain.table:
DrugRibosomal targetStep blocked
Aminoglycosides30S (irreversible)Initiation, mRNA misreading
Tetracyclines30S (reversible)tRNA attachment at the A site
Macrolides50STranslocation
Clindamycin50SPeptidyl transferase
Linezolid50S (23S rRNA)70S initiation complex
why: Cytochrome enzyme inhibition is the erythromycin and clarithromycin interaction, not linezolid's.
QT prolongation is a fluoroquinolone and macrolide effect and would not cause clonus or hyperreflexia.
Linezolid marrow suppression is mainly thrombocytopenia after about 2 weeks, not a neuromuscular picture at day 2.
Lactic acidosis is a rare linezolid effect, but it does not explain tremor, hyperreflexia and clonus.
explain.takeaway: Linezolid binds 23S rRNA to block the 70S initiation complex, covers MRSA and VRE, and causes serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs because of weak MAO inhibition.

explain.objective: Recognize clinically important antibiotic drug-drug interactions

questions.stem:
A 41-year-old man with advanced HIV infection and a CD4 count of 60/microL has progressive dyspnea and a dry cough. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows cysts of a fungal organism on silver stain. He is started on the antibiotic combination the lecture lists for this pneumonia. On day 5 his labs are drawn.

[[labs 0]]

The abnormal potassium is a known effect of this drug, which also covers which organism?
choices: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Bacteroides fragilis
Nocardia species
Enterococcus faecium
Mycoplasma pneumoniae

explain.html:
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an antifolate with an unusual spectrum. It covers Gram-positives including MRSA, Gram-negatives such as E. coli, Klebsiella and Stenotrophomonas but no Pseudomonas, and a group of others: Pneumocystis, Nocardia and Listeria. It is used for skin and soft tissue infections and PCP pneumonia. Its adverse effects are nephrotoxicity (crystalluria), hyperkalemia, bone marrow suppression, photosensitivity, rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Silver-staining cysts in a man with HIV and a CD4 count of 60 are Pneumocystis, so he is on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. A potassium of 6.2 on day 5 is its listed hyperkalemia. Of the choices, only Nocardia is in its spectrum.
why: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole has no Pseudomonas activity.
Anaerobes such as B. fragilis are not in its spectrum; metronidazole covers them.
Vancomycin-resistant E. faecium is not covered by trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Atypicals such as Mycoplasma are covered by macrolides, tetracyclines and respiratory fluoroquinolones, not by this drug.
explain.takeaway: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treats Pneumocystis pneumonia and covers MRSA, Nocardia, Listeria and Stenotrophomonas but not Pseudomonas, and hyperkalemia is a key adverse effect.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Describe the general spectrum of activity

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old woman has a frothy, malodorous vaginal discharge, and a wet mount shows motile flagellated protozoa. She is treated with a drug that is a prodrug: it becomes active only when its nitro group is reduced inside anaerobic bacteria and protozoa, forming free radicals that damage DNA. That weekend she drinks wine at a party and develops flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting and palpitations.

Which explanation and additional fact about this drug are correct?
choices: An IgE reaction to the drug; it also covers MRSA well
Histamine release from fast dosing; it also treats Pneumocystis
Serotonin syndrome; it also covers vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus
A disulfiram-like reaction; it also treats C. difficile
QT prolongation; it also covers atypical respiratory pathogens

explain.html:
Metronidazole, a nitroimidazole, is a prodrug activated by reduction of its nitro group inside anaerobic bacteria and protozoa, where it forms toxic free radicals that damage DNA; it is bactericidal. Because activation needs anaerobic metabolism, its spectrum is anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium) and protozoa (Giardia, Trichomonas, Entamoeba). It is used for intra-abdominal infections, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis and C. difficile. Its adverse effects are GI upset, metallic taste, peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.

Frothy discharge with motile flagellated protozoa is Trichomonas, and flushing, headache, nausea and palpitations after wine is the disulfiram-like reaction. Patients should avoid alcohol during therapy. Of the paired facts, only C. difficile is a listed use.
explain.table:
FeatureMetronidazole
ActivationNitro group reduced in anaerobes and protozoa
CoversAnaerobes; Giardia, Trichomonas, Entamoeba
UsesIntra-abdominal infection, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, C. difficile
Adverse effectsGI upset, metallic taste, neuropathy, disulfiram-like reaction
why: Flushing after alcohol is a drug-alcohol reaction, not allergy, and metronidazole does not cover aerobes such as MRSA.
Infusion-related histamine release is vancomycin, and Pneumocystis is treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Serotonin syndrome and VRE coverage describe linezolid, and the trigger here was alcohol.
Metronidazole has no atypical coverage, and QT prolongation belongs to fluoroquinolones and macrolides.
explain.takeaway: Metronidazole is a prodrug reduced in anaerobes and protozoa to DNA-damaging radicals; it treats anaerobic infections, trichomoniasis and C. difficile and causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.

explain.objective: Recognize major or very common side effects

questions.stem:
A new oral antibacterial, drug X, inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. It is nearly completely absorbed, has a large volume of distribution, and penetrates lung, bone and abdominal tissue well. It is cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism; less than a fifth of each dose appears unchanged in the urine. In vitro it is active against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Legionella, Bacteroides fragilis, Escherichia coli and Shigella, but not Pseudomonas. Five patients with normal kidney and liver function each have an infection whose isolate tests susceptible to drug X, and a resident argues its wide tissue penetration means it will work in all of them.

Which patient's infection is drug X least likely to cure?
choices: A child with bloody diarrhea due to Shigella
A woman with acute cystitis due to E. coli
A man with an abdominal abscess due to Bacteroides and E. coli
A woman with Legionella pneumonia and diarrhea
A man with lobar pneumonia due to pneumococcus

explain.html:
A drug that kills well in the laboratory is useless at a site it does not reach, so site of infection is part of choosing the drug. For the urinary tract, the deciding property is the route of elimination: renally excreted drugs are concentrated in urine, while drugs cleared by hepatic metabolism leave little active drug there. The fluoroquinolones show this inside one class: ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin are renally excreted and used for UTIs, but moxifloxacin, hepatically metabolized, does not reach adequate urinary concentrations and is not used for UTIs. Tetracyclines are another example, distributing widely except into CSF and urine.

Drug X behaves like moxifloxacin: excellent absorption and wide tissue penetration, strong Gram-positive, atypical and anaerobic activity, but hepatic clearance with under a fifth in urine. The resident's argument from wide tissue penetration is the red herring, since urine is a compartment filled by excretion, not by distribution. Every other patient's infection is in a tissue the drug reaches with an organism it covers, so cystitis is where it fails.
explain.table:
Property of drug XWhat it predicts
Excellent oral absorption, wide tissue distributionGood levels in blood, lung, abdomen
Cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism, under a fifth excreted unchanged in urineLow urinary concentration: fails in the bladder
Strong Gram-positive, atypical and anaerobic activityCovers pneumococcus, Legionella, Bacteroides
Enterobacterales and GI pathogen activityCovers E. coli, Shigella
why: Shigella is a covered GI pathogen and gut tissue levels do not depend on urinary excretion.
Anaerobic and Enterobacterales activity with good abdominal penetration suit this abscess.
Drug X covers atypicals and reaches the lung, so Legionella pneumonia fits it.
Drug X penetrates lung and is active against pneumococcus, like the respiratory fluoroquinolones.
explain.takeaway: Drugs cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism (for example moxifloxacin) do not reach adequate urinary concentrations and should not be used for UTIs, even when the isolate is susceptible.
explain.topic: Route of elimination decides urinary efficacy

explain.objective: Recommend appropriate antibiotic therapy based on site of infection and suspected or actual bacterial pathogens

questions.stem:
In a laboratory study, two protein synthesis inhibitors that bind the same ribosomal subunit are tested against a Gram-negative rod. Drug A binds its target reversibly; while it is present, colony counts stay flat, and after the drug is washed out, growth resumes within an hour. Drug B binds its target irreversibly; colony counts fall about 1,000-fold, the fall is faster when a higher peak concentration is used, and growth stays suppressed for several hours after washout even though no measurable drug remains. Drug B is poorly absorbed from the gut. Drug A is well absorbed by mouth.

Drug B most likely shares which additional property?
choices: It causes a disulfiram-like reaction when alcohol is consumed
It inhibits hepatic CYP enzymes and raises other drug levels
It is synergistic with cell wall agents against enterococci
It causes serotonin syndrome with serotonergic antidepressants
Absorption falls when it is taken with milk or antacids

explain.html:
Two drug classes bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and behave very differently. Aminoglycosides bind it irreversibly, block the initiation complex, cause misreading of mRNA and disrupt membrane integrity, so they are bactericidal, with concentration-dependent killing and a prolonged post-antibiotic effect; used alone they act only on Gram-negative rods, and they are synergistic with beta-lactams or vancomycin against Gram-positives because cell wall damage increases their entry. Tetracyclines bind 30S reversibly and block aminoacyl-tRNA at the A site, so they are bacteriostatic and are chelated by milk, antacids and iron.

In this experiment drug B kills, binds irreversibly, kills faster at higher peaks, and suppresses growth after washout, which is an aminoglycoside. Drug A is the tetracycline, and the shared subunit is the red herring that pulls students toward the chelation answer. Knowing the killing pattern explains why gentamicin is paired with ampicillin for enterococcal endocarditis.
explain.table:
FeatureAminoglycosidesTetracyclines
Ribosomal target30S, irreversible30S, reversible
EffectMisreading of mRNA; bactericidalBlock tRNA at A site; bacteriostatic
Killing patternConcentration dependent, prolonged PAEGrowth halts while drug present
Key pearlSynergy with cell wall agents for Gram-positivesChelated by milk, antacids, iron
why: The disulfiram-like reaction is metronidazole, which forms free radicals that damage DNA and does not bind ribosomes.
CYP inhibition is a macrolide trait, and macrolides bind 50S and are bacteriostatic.
Serotonin syndrome is linezolid, a bacteriostatic 50S binder with weak MAO inhibitor activity.
Chelation by milk and antacids is the tetracycline property, and the tetracycline here is drug A.
explain.takeaway: Aminoglycosides bind 30S irreversibly and are bactericidal with concentration-dependent killing and a post-antibiotic effect; against Gram-positives such as Enterococcus they require a cell wall agent for synergy.
